title: Duke's scores on paper, odd voicings and why studio writing loses personalities
summary: Tom Whaley's copying, Duke putting the baritone in the middle, and Ella's arrangement sounding vanilla with another orchestra.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Yes, that's right. That's very true, because there was one time I was doing some things with Johnny Hodges, you know, with a small group, about eight or ten pieces, and Tom Whaley -- Duke was living next door to me, and Tom Whaley was living about, oh, maybe three blocks away, and Billy Strayhorn. We were all living in one area. So I had to

take these scores over to Tom's to get them copied, and Tom says, "Take a look at this. This is one of Duke's scores." And I looked at it, and I said, "Tom, this can't work." He said, "You've been listening to it for the last 25 years."
But you can't hear it when it's played, you know? I looked at it on paper and I said, "This thing is supposed to work, man."
He says, "It's what I'm here for." I said, "But it doesn't sound like that when they play it." He said, "No, but that's what's there."

And Strayhorn told me that Duke taught him extremes. Like he would put Carney's (PHONETIC) -- the baritone, normally everybody puts the baritone on the bottom, but he would put Paul on the bottom and put Carney up in the middle of the section and get a completely different sound. Put him in, you know, different, odd registers. You know? And those guys had great sounds. Oh, they had -- they all had great tones, you know? And I may have said this before -- I think I did say it before -- I had written this thing for -- it was really for Ella and just for Duke, on the -- "Ella At Duke's Place." And Ella liked the arrangement very much, but she didn't realize I was voicing like the old man, you know?

And she took the arrangement to some other orchestra and I heard it and I said, "Ella take that out of the book, because it doesn't sound good. It sounds like, you know, it sounds very like what we call vanilla." Just nothing, you know. Because if you don't have a Harry Carney or a Johnny Hodges Gonzalves in there and Paul Gonzales and all that, it doesn't mean anything. The personalities are not there. And --
Well, Duke definitely wrote for the sound of the individual.
Yeah. And I did the same way. But that's the objection I have to studio writing, even though that's instant music, sight reading and everything.

But you don't get those personalities in there. You know, you don't get the personalities, and it makes it harder on the arranger, because you have to put your own thing into it to make it a little fresh or different, you know?
You have to do it from the manuscript.
Because normally if you do it like with Ellington's thing, well he did it with the manuscript but he had the players to do it too. You know, that made quite a difference.
